title: Threshold Behavior of ZX and ZY Surface Codes Under Circuit-Level Biased and Crosstalk Noise
abstract: Studying the threshold behavior of surface codes under biased noise models is an active area of research. Previous work Tuckett et al. (2018), using an optimal tensor-network decoder, demonstrated that replacing $Z$-type stabilizers with $Y$-type stabilizers significantly improves the surface code threshold under code-capacity level dephasing noise. In this work, we construct and study a $ZY$ surface code by replacing the $X$-type stabilizers with $Y$-type stabilizers. We compare it with the standard $ZX$ surface code under circuit-level Pauli-$X$ biased noise, with and without an additional gate-based $XX$ crosstalk noise. We find that for the $ZX$ surface code, the $X$-memory threshold increases monotonically with bias while the $Z$-memory threshold decreases and saturates. For the $ZY$ surface code, the $Y$-memory threshold is nearly constant across all bias values. The $Z$-memory thresholds of the $ZX$ and $ZY$ codes are consistent within the uncertainty. Adding $XX$ crosstalk reduces the $Z$-memory threshold beyond the fitting uncertainty while leaving the $X$ memory threshold largely unaffected. The choice of CNOT ordering redistributes threshold performance between the two logical memories. Our work extends prior observations from code-capacity level noise to circuit-level noise. It also indicates the need for decoders capable of jointly reasoning over correlated syndrome information so that tailored stabilizer structures could be fully utilized for quantum error correction.
summary: This work analyzes how tailored surface codes, specifically comparing ZX and ZY variants, perform under realistic circuit-level noise, including bias and crosstalk. The study finds that while the ZY code theoretically captures more error information, current matching decoders fail to utilize this correlation. Ultimately, the paper stresses the need for advanced decoders capable of handling complex, correlated syndrome data.
main_problem: The study investigates the threshold behavior of tailored surface codes (ZX and ZY) when subjected to realistic circuit-level biased and crosstalk noise.
main_result: The ZY code shows a Y-memory threshold nearly constant across bias, while the ZX code shows an increasing X-memory threshold with bias; furthermore, the analysis highlights that standard decoders cannot fully utilize the correlated syndrome information available in the ZY structure.
method: The authors simulate performance using the minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoder, comparing results across varying bias parameters and incorporating crosstalk noise.
model_or_system: The system uses surface codes, comparing the standard ZX code against a constructed ZY code (replacing X-stabilizers with Y-stabilizers). Noise models include Pauli-X biased noise and additional gate-based XX crosstalk noise, moving beyond idealized code-capacity noise.
key_observables: Memory thresholds ($p_{X}^{th}, p_{Z}^{th}, p_{Y}^{th}$) for X, Y, and Z logical memories, and the logical error rate ($p_L$).
important_parameters: Bias parameter ($\eta$), crosstalk probability ($p_x$), and code distance ($d$).
main_assumptions: The primary limitation is that the MWPM decoder cannot process the correlated syndrome information generated by the ZY code, which forms a hypergraph structure.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the 2D structure of the unrotated surface code with Z and X stabilizers, while Figure 2 shows the stabilizer measurement circuits for Z, X, and Y stabilizers.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the problem of circuit-level noise, then comparing the threshold behavior of ZX and ZY codes under biased noise, analyzing the effect of crosstalk, and finally discussing the limitations of current matching decoders for the complex syndrome structure of the ZY code.
why_interesting: The detailed analysis of how specific stabilizer structures (ZY vs ZX) interact with directional noise biases and crosstalk provides concrete, actionable insights for designing more robust quantum error correction protocols.

figures.caption: Figure 1: A two-dimensional implementation of unrotated surface code with Z-type (green) and X-type (yellow) stabilizers. Each filled circle (•) denotes a measurement qubit, and each open circle (◦) denotes a data qubit. Each data qubit is surrounded by four measurement qubits and each measurement qubit is connected to four data qubits to perform syndrome extraction using the circuits shown in Fig. 2.

Figure 2: Stabilizer measurement circuits of the Z stabilizer (a), X stabilizer (b), and Y stabilizer (c). Each filled circle (•) is the measurement qubit, that acts as an ancilla and performs repeated rounds of controlled operation on four data qubits to give parity information. That parity information helps us find out if an error occurred in the surface code. In the circuits, |g⟩represents ground state initialization in the computational basis, and I on the ancilla of (a) denotes idle step when the ancilla for X checks and Y checks undergo H gate. The box with arrow at the end of each circuit denotes measurement in computational basis, and Ψ denotes the possible outcomes from the circuit.

Figure 3: (a) Representations of syndrome extraction circuits for X-type stabilizer (upper diagram) and Z-type stabilizer (lower diagram). The upper most qubit in both circuits in (a) are measurement qubits that act as ancilla qubits, and the following four qubits are data qubits whose parity is measured by the circuit. (b) and (c) denote the order of performing CNOT gate in unrotated and rotated codes respectively. This figure shows 10231203 CNOT order, where the first four digits denote the order of CNOT operations in X-type stabilizer measurement circuit and the later four digits represent the order of CNOT operations in Z-type stabilizer measurement circuit.
